items.finding: Multilocular intraretinal cystoid spaces; foveal thickening; systemic diabetes with haemorrhages and hard exudates.
items.reason: Remember: diabetic macular edema on OCT shows multilocular intraretinal cysts in the inner and outer nuclear layers, and centre-involved disease is treated with anti-VEGF therapy.

items.finding: Multiple dome-shaped sub-RPE elevations; preserved overlying neurosensory retina; no subretinal fluid or neovascular membrane; mild hyperreflectivity beneath the RPE consistent with drusen remodelling.
items.reason: Remember: large drusen (greater than 125 micrometres) with or without pigmentary change define intermediate AMD, and the AREDS2 supplement plus smoking cessation are the key modifiable measures.

items.finding: Dome-shaped RPE detachment; subretinal hyporeflective space; disruption of outer retinal layers at the fovea; age over 70 with drusen and pigmentary change.
items.reason: Remember: Late AMD on OCT = RPE elevation or atrophy plus outer retinal disruption in an older adult with drusen; geographic atrophy is the dry form and CNV is the wet form.

items.finding: Intraretinal cystoid spaces in the central macula; thickened inner and outer nuclear layers; diabetic history with hard exudates and microaneurysms.
items.reason: Remember: Diabetic macular edema is intraretinal cystic fluid on OCT in a diabetic patient, and central subfield thickness guides anti-VEGF treatment.

items.finding: Dome-shaped RPE elevation with heterogeneous sub-RPE content; drusen on fundus; age over 70 with metamorphopsia; intact foveal pit without full-thickness defect.
items.reason: Remember: a dome-shaped sub-RPE elevation in an older patient with drusen points to late AMD (pigment epithelial detachment or neovascular change), not central serous chorioretinopathy.

items.finding: Large dome-shaped RPE elevation; multiple hyporeflective intraretinal and subretinal cysts; disruption of the foveal contour; patient age over 70 with painless metamorphopsia.
items.reason: Remember: Late AMD on OCT shows RPE elevation (pigment epithelial detachment), intraretinal or subretinal fluid and cysts, and subretinal fibrosis or atrophy; age over 50 with painless central vision loss and metamorphopsia is the classic presentation.

items.finding: Hyperreflective membrane on the inner retinal surface; wrinkled inner retinal layers; distorted foveal pit with intact outer retina.
items.reason: Remember: a hyperreflective inner retinal membrane with wrinkling and an intact outer retina on OCT is an epiretinal membrane, the commonest cause of macular pucker.

items.finding: Hyperreflective band on the inner retinal surface; corrugated and folded inner retina; intact foveal contour without full-thickness defect; cellophane-like macular reflex on fundus examination.
items.reason: Remember: Epiretinal membrane on OCT appears as a hyperreflective inner surface band with retinal corrugation and preserved foveal architecture, and it is treated with vitrectomy and membrane peeling when vision is significantly affected.

items.finding: Hyperreflective band on the inner retinal surface; corrugated inner retinal layers; preserved foveal pit; no sub-retinal fluid; glistening macular sheen clinically.
items.reason: Remember: epiretinal membrane shows a hyperreflective inner surface band with retinal wrinkling and an intact foveal pit, causing metamorphopsia with preserved or mildly reduced vision.

items.finding: Diffuse retinal thickening, loss of foveal depression, intraretinal fluid, dilated tortuous veins, scattered intraretinal haemorrhages, hypertension history.
items.reason: Remember: retinal vein occlusion with macular oedema shows diffuse intraretinal thickening with loss of the foveal depression on OCT, and always look for systemic hypertension, diabetes, and glaucoma as risk factors.

items.finding: Multiple large, confluent intraretinal cysts in the macula; intact foveal architecture; clinical hypertension with haemorrhages and venous dilatation in all four quadrants.
items.reason: Remember: in retinal vein occlusion, cystoid macular oedema is the commonest cause of central vision loss, and it is treated first-line with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy.

items.finding: Cystoid hyporeflective spaces in the macula, disorganised inner retinal layers, thinned and attenuated outer retina, undulating foveal contour, and the clinical pattern of diffuse flame hemorrhages with tortuous veins.
items.reason: Remember: in late retinal vein occlusion the OCT shows chronic cystoid macular edema, disorganised inner retina and outer retinal atrophy, so think of venous occlusion when diffuse hemorrhages and tortuosity coexist with macular cysts.

items.finding: Cystic hyporeflective intraretinal spaces in a thickened macula; sudden painless visual loss; diffuse haemorrhages and dilated tortuous veins in all four quadrants; hypertensive older patient.
items.reason: Remember: diffuse haemorrhages in all four quadrants plus tortuous veins suggest CRVO, and cystic intraretinal spaces on OCT indicate CME, the main cause of visual loss in RVO.

items.finding: Full-thickness foveal defect on OCT; separated edges with elevated retinal cuff; loss of foveal pit; age-related vitreous liquefaction with metamorphopsia.
items.reason: Remember: a full-thickness macular hole on OCT shows a full-thickness foveal defect with the edges separated, and vitreomacular traction is a key cause that is often treated with vitrectomy.

items.finding: Full-thickness defect from ILM to RPE; rolled hole edges; premacular cuff; loss of foveal depression.
items.reason: Remember: a full-thickness macular hole is a full-thickness foveal defect with a premacular cuff, and vitrectomy with ILM peeling is the standard treatment.

items.finding: Taut hyperreflective vitreous strand attached to the fovea; focal foveal elevation with intraretinal cystoid spaces; no full-thickness foveal defect; posterior hyaloid still adherent to macula.
items.reason: Remember: vitreomacular traction is an incomplete posterior vitreous detachment with a taut vitreous strand attached to the fovea, and it is the key precursor lesion to full-thickness macular hole.

items.finding: Enlarged cup with a large cup-to-disc ratio; thinned and notched neuroretinal rim; nasal displacement of vessels (bayonetting); asymmetry relative to the fellow eye.
items.reason: Remember: in glaucoma, the disc changes (rim thinning, notching, enlarged cup, vessel bayonetting) precede visual field loss, so a cup-to-disc ratio asymmetry above 0.2 between the eyes warrants full glaucoma work-up even with a normal IOP.

items.finding: Enlarged pale cup; focal inferior and superior rim thinning; nasal displacement of vessels as they bend over the rim; raised IOP of 26 mmHg.
items.reason: Remember: a deep, enlarged cup with focal rim notching and nasal vessel bayoneting in a patient with raised IOP points to glaucomatous optic neuropathy.

items.finding: Enlarged pale cup; thinned inferior and superior neuroretinal rim; nasal displacement of retinal vessels over disc edge.
items.reason: Remember: Glaucomatous optic neuropathy is a structural diagnosis; a large cup with thinned rim and nasal vessel displacement signals damage even when intraocular pressure is only borderline raised.

items.finding: Large cup-to-disc ratio, thinned inferior and superior rim, vessel bayoneting at the disc margin, and a corresponding arcuate visual field defect with elevated IOP.
items.reason: Remember: a large cup-to-disc ratio with rim thinning and vessel bayoneting in a patient with raised IOP or an arcuate field defect means glaucoma until proven otherwise.

items.finding: Enlarged pale cup; thinned, notched inferior or superior rim; vessel bayoneting; raised IOP with family history.
items.reason: Remember: glaucomatous optic neuropathy is recognised by increased cup-to-disc ratio, focal rim thinning or notching, and bayoneting of vessels; IOP lowering is the only proven treatment.

items.finding: Sharp, pink optic disc with normal cup-to-disc ratio; normal vessel calibre and arcade pattern; clear foveal reflex with no hard exudates or haemorrhages.
items.reason: Remember: Normal retina with a clear disc, normal vessels and no microaneurysms or haemorrhages equals no diabetic retinopathy, so routine annual screening is sufficient.

items.finding: Small red dots (microaneurysms) in the posterior pole; absence of flame haemorrhages, cotton wool spots, venous beading, and new vessels; normal optic disc and macular appearance.
items.reason: Remember: mild NPDR = microaneurysms only; the first clinical sign of diabetic retinopathy is the microaneurysm, and the moment haemorrhages beyond minimal number, cotton wool spots, or venous beading appear, the grade becomes moderate.

items.finding: Scattered dot-and-blot haemorrhages and yellowish hard exudates in the posterior pole; absence of new vessels on the optic disc; no vitreous or pre-retinal haemorrhage.
items.reason: Remember: Moderate NPDR = microaneurysms plus dot-and-blot haemorrhages or hard exudates in more than one quadrant, but no severe NPDR or PDR features (4-2-1 rule for severe NPDR: haemorrhages in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2, IRMA in 1).

items.finding: Yellow hard exudates clustered in the temporal macula and arcade; scattered dot-and-blot haemorrhages; absence of new vessels on the optic disc or retina.
items.reason: Remember: Moderate NPDR = more than microaneurysms only (haemorrhages, hard exudates, or cotton wool spots) but less than severe criteria; Severe NPDR needs 4-2-1 rule findings (haemorrhages in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2 quadrants, or IRMA in 1 quadrant).

items.finding: Multiple dot and blot haemorrhages, scattered hard exudates, and microaneurysms in the posterior pole; absence of neovascularisation on the disc or elsewhere; no preretinal or vitreous haemorrhage.
items.reason: Remember: Mild NPDR = microaneurysms only; Moderate NPDR = haemorrhages, microaneurysms, and/or exudates beyond mild but short of severe; Severe NPDR = 4-2-1 rule; PDR = neovascularisation.

items.finding: Dot and blot haemorrhages; temporal hard exudates; cotton-wool spots; absence of new vessels on the disc.
items.reason: Remember: Moderate NPDR = more than microaneurysms only (haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots) but not meeting severe NPDR criteria; no neovascularisation.

items.finding: Yellow sharply demarcated hard exudates in the temporal macula; scattered dot and blot haemorrhages; absence of new vessels on the optic disc or retina.
items.reason: Remember: moderate NPDR = more than microaneurysms only, with dot/blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, or cotton wool spots in fewer than four quadrants, and no neovascularisation.

items.finding: Dot and blot haemorrhages in all four quadrants; venous beading in more than two quadrants; cotton-wool spots and hard exudates; absence of new vessels on the disc or retina.
items.reason: Remember the 4-2-1 rule: haemorrhages and microaneurysms in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2 or more quadrants, or IRMA in 1 quadrant defines severe NPDR, with about 50 percent risk of progression to PDR within 1 year.

items.finding: Multiple dot and blot hemorrhages across quadrants; hard exudates near the macula; absence of new vessels at the optic disc.
items.reason: Remember the 4-2-1 rule: severe NPDR = more than 20 hemorrhages in 4 quadrants, OR definite venous beading in 2 or more quadrants, OR prominent IRMA in 1 or more quadrant; any of these without neovascularisation makes it severe NPDR with about 50 percent one-year progression risk

items.finding: Multiple quadrant dot and blot haemorrhages; venous beading; temporal macular hard exudates with no new vessels.
items.reason: Remember the 4-2-1 rule: haemorrhages in 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2 quadrants, or IRMA in 1 quadrant defines severe NPDR, with a high risk of progression to PDR within a year.

items.finding: Fibrovascular membrane at the posterior pole, preretinal and vitreous haemorrhage, yellow exudates, and a diabetic history.
items.reason: Remember: Proliferative means new vessels (NVD, NVE) or vitreous or preretinal haemorrhage; treat with panretinal photocoagulation or anti-VEGF.

items.finding: Fine new vessels with fibrovascular tissue at the optic disc; cotton-wool spots; scattered intraretinal haemorrhages; history of poorly controlled diabetes.
items.reason: Remember: new vessels on the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE), or vitreous/preretinal haemorrhage, define PDR and mandate PRP or anti-VEGF.

items.finding: Fine new vessels at the optic disc; large dark clumped haemorrhages; cotton-wool spots; hard exudates; tortuous dilated veins.
items.reason: Remember: any neovascularisation of the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE) equals PDR, regardless of how few haemorrhages are present; the 4-2-1 rule identifies high-risk severe NPDR, which is one step from PDR.

items.finding: Continuous retinal vascularisation to the periphery; no visible demarcation line or ridge; normal calibre posterior pole vessels; visible optic disc and macula.
items.reason: Remember: at 28 weeks gestation, screening is mandatory, and a normal fundus with full posterior vascularisation indicates no ROP, but rescreening is still required because risk persists.

items.finding: Confluent pale-orange laser scars; sharp demarcation between vascular and avascular retina; tortuous posterior pole vessels; preterm birth at 24 weeks.
items.reason: Remember: laser scars with a demarcated avascular peripheral retina in a preterm infant indicate laser-treated ROP, and follow-up is essential because late recurrence and retinal detachment can still occur.

items.finding: Funnel-shaped retinal fold converging on the optic nerve; large retrolental fibrovascular membrane; total detachment of the retina; preretinal and vitreous haemorrhage.
items.reason: Remember: Stage 4 is partial detachment, Stage 5 is total funnel detachment; the funnel shape and disc displacement toward the lens define Stage 5 and signal a poor visual outcome.

items.finding: Enlarged disc with increased central excavation; pale thinned neuroretinal rim; raised IOP of 26 mmHg with normal visual acuity.
items.reason: Remember: in glaucoma, the cup enlarges and the neuroretinal rim thins, typically in the inferior and superior poles first (ISNT rule violated), and a vertical CDR above 0.6 or asymmetry greater than 0.2 is highly suspicious.

items.finding: Oval disc with oblique long axis; temporal crescent of visible choroid; intact neuroretinal rim without notching or pallor.
items.reason: Remember: a tilted disc is oval, obliquely oriented, with a temporal crescent and an intact rim; it is benign, often seen with high myopia, and must not be mistaken for glaucoma.

items.finding: Oval, obliquely oriented disc; inferonasal displacement of the retinal vessels; temporal crescent of pale peripapillary tissue; no disc swelling or hemorrhage.
items.reason: Remember: Tilted disc is oblique and oval with inferonasal vessel displacement, is congenital, is often seen in myopia, and is usually benign.

items.finding: Fleshy vascularised membrane covering the entire corneal surface; history of chemical injury; progressive visual loss and photophobia.
items.reason: Remember: a conjunctival membrane covering the whole cornea with vessels indicates corneal conjunctivalization from limbal stem cell deficiency, a surgical emergency that threatens vision.

items.finding: Tortuous, dilated veins in all quadrants; extensive deep blot and flame hemorrhages; severe optic disc edema and hyperemia.
items.reason: Remember: CRVO shows venous engorgement and hemorrhages in all four quadrants (blood and thunder pattern), whereas BRVO involves a single quadrant and CRAO shows a pale retina with a cherry-red spot.

items.finding: Corrugated retinal elevation over three quadrants; large superotemporal retinal break; extension toward the macula; history of photopsia, shadow curtain, and high myopia.
items.reason: Remember: a corrugated, elevated retina with a visible retinal break in a myope with photopsia and a shadow curtain is rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, a sight-threatening emergency requiring urgent repair.

items.finding: Bone-spicule pigment in the mid-periphery; arteriolar attenuation; waxy pale optic disc; young patient with night blindness.
items.reason: Remember: Triad of retinitis pigmentosa = night blindness, peripheral (concentric) field constriction and bone-spicule pigmentation, with arteriolar attenuation and waxy disc pallor; ERG shows reduced or absent rod responses.

items.finding: Complete foveal discontinuity from ILM to RPE; intraretinal cystoid change at the hole margins; elevated fluid at the edges of the defect.
items.reason: Remember: a full-thickness macular hole is a complete break from ILM to RPE at the fovea, classically caused by vitreofoveal traction and treated with vitrectomy, ILM peeling, and gas tamponade.

items.finding: Undulating elevations of the hyperreflective RPE band; reduced reflectivity beneath the elevations; intact inner retinal layers; absence of subretinal or intraretinal fluid; yellow discrete macular deposits clinically.
items.reason: Remember: drusen appear on OCT as undulating elevations of the hyperreflective RPE band with reduced reflectivity beneath, and AREDS2 supplementation is the established treatment for intermediate or advanced dry AMD.

items.finding: Smooth foveal contour with preserved foveal pit; continuous, evenly thick retinal layers; no intraretinal cysts, subretinal fluid, or surface membrane.
items.reason: Remember: a normal macular OCT shows a preserved foveal depression with well-defined, evenly thick retinal layers and no intraretinal or subretinal fluid.

items.finding: Intraretinal cystoid spaces; central retinal thickening; diabetic history with hard exudates and microaneurysms.
items.reason: Remember: diabetic macular edema on OCT shows intraretinal cystoid spaces and central subfield thickening; anti-VEGF is first-line when the fovea is involved.

items.finding: Hyper-reflective band on the inner retinal surface; irregular inner retinal contour; preserved foveal depression without full-thickness break.
items.reason: Remember: epiretinal membrane shows a hyper-reflective surface band with retinal wrinkling on OCT, causing metamorphopsia, whereas a macular hole shows a full-thickness foveal break.

items.finding: Intraretinal cystic hyporeflective spaces; central subfield thickening with effaced foveal pit; diabetic microaneurysms and hard exudates on fundus.
items.reason: Remember: DME is the commonest cause of vision loss in DR, and OCT intraretinal cystoid spaces with central subfield thickening are the key imaging sign.

items.finding: Thick uniform rim, small cup with CDR below 0.5, sharp margins, normal vessel course, no peripapillary atrophy, normal IOP and open angles.
items.reason: Remember: a healthy disc has a thick, uniform neuroretinal rim (ISNT rule: inferior is greater than superior is greater than nasal is greater than temporal) and a cup-to-disc ratio below 0.5 with no notching or splinter haemorrhage.

items.finding: Pink and uniform neuroretinal rim; small central physiological cup; vessels with normal course over the margin without bayoneting; no haemorrhage, pallor, or notching.
items.reason: Remember: a healthy disc has an intact, pink, uniformly thick neuroretinal rim (ISNT rule: inferior is thickest, then superior, nasal, temporal) with a small physiological cup.

items.finding: Uniform pink neuroretinal rim; small central physiological cup; normal radial vessel course without notching or haemorrhage.
items.reason: Remember: A healthy disc has a uniform, pink neuroretinal rim following the ISNT rule, a small symmetric cup, and a CDR below 0.3 with no notching or haemorrhage; any focal rim loss or disc haemorrhage should prompt glaucoma evaluation.

items.finding: Intact pink neuroretinal rim; small central cup with vertical cup-to-disc ratio about 0.3; no notching, disc haemorrhage, or RNFL defect; normal IOP and full visual fields.
items.reason: Remember: a healthy disc has an intact ISNT rim, a small physiologic cup, and no notching or disc haemorrhage; always correlate the disc appearance with IOP, visual fields, and RNFL imaging before diagnosing glaucoma.

items.finding: Clues: uniform pink neuroretinal rim obeying ISNT; small physiological cup of about 0.3; normal vessel course without nasalisation; no notching, pallor, or disc haemorrhage; normal IOP and vision.
items.reason: Remember: a healthy disc has an ISNT-compliant rim (inferior is greater than superior is greater than nasal is greater than temporal), a cup-to-disc ratio under about 0.5, and symmetric discs between the two eyes.

items.finding: Uniform pink neuroretinal rim; small cup (cup-to-disc about 0.3); vessels not displaced or bent; no notching, peripapillary atrophy or disc haemorrhage; normal IOP and visual acuity.
items.reason: Remember: a healthy disc has an intact ISNT-patterned rim and a small, symmetric cup (cup-to-disc ratio below 0.5 with no asymmetry); diagnose glaucoma only with structural rim loss plus corresponding OCT or visual field defect.

items.finding: Pink uniform neuroretinal rim; small symmetric cup; sharp disc margin with normal vessel course; no notching or haemorrhage.
items.reason: Remember: a healthy disc has a pink, intact neuroretinal rim following the ISNT rule, a small symmetric cup-to-disc ratio, and no notching, haemorrhage, or peripapillary atrophy.

items.finding: Deep pale cup, thinned and notched inferior and superior rim, nasal displacement of the retinal vessels, asymmetric cup-to-disc ratio.
items.reason: Remember: glaucomatous optic neuropathy shows an increased cup-to-disc ratio with rim thinning and notching, and the ISNT rule (inferior, superior, nasal, temporal rim thickness) is usually violated.

items.finding: Enlarged pale cup; thinned rim, especially inferior and superior; raised IOP of 26 mmHg; family history.
items.reason: Remember: glaucomatous optic neuropathy is defined by structural loss of the neuroretinal rim and an enlarged cup, not by IOP alone.

items.finding: Enlarged cup-to-disc ratio; thinned inferior and superior neuroretinal rim; pale excavated centre with vessel bending.
items.reason: Remember: glaucomatous optic neuropathy = large pale cup, thinned inferior and superior rim (ISNT rule), with the cup-to-disc ratio greater than 0.6 suggesting disease.

items.finding: Enlarged pale cup; thinned inferotemporal and superotemporal neuroretinal rim; nasal displacement and bayoneting of retinal vessels.
items.reason: Remember: in glaucoma the cup enlarges and the neuroretinal rim thins, with vessels bending nasally at the disc edge; the disc is pale and excavated, not swollen.

items.finding: Large pale cup occupying most of the disc; thinned inferior and superior rim; vessels displaced nasally and bending sharply over the cup margin.
items.reason: Remember: a large, pale, excavated cup with bayoneting of vessels and asymmetry between eyes indicates glaucomatous optic neuropathy until proven otherwise.

items.finding: Healthy optic disc with clear rim; normal macula without exudates; normal vessel calibre without beading or new vessels; no haemorrhages.
items.reason: Remember: No DR means zero microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, cotton wool spots, venous beading, IRMA, or neovascularisation; long diabetes duration alone does not imply retinopathy.

items.finding: Normal optic disc rim; no microaneurysms or dot-blot haemorrhages; no hard exudates or cotton-wool spots; no IRMA, venous beading, or new vessels.
items.reason: Remember: no diabetic retinopathy means a normal fundus with no microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, IRMA, venous beading, or new vessels; a single microaneurysm alone upgrades the grade to mild NPDR.

items.finding: Normal optic disc margins; uniform red reflex without haemorrhage; no hard exudates or cotton wool spots; clear macula.
items.reason: Remember: No DR means no microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, or neovascularisation on fundus examination; screen again in 12 months for diabetics with no retinopathy.

items.finding: Clear optic disc with normal rim; normal vascular arcades without venous beading; no haemorrhages, exudates, or cotton-wool spots; normal foveal region without oedema.
items.reason: Remember: no DR means no microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates, cotton-wool spots, venous beading, IRMA, or neovascularisation on fundus photography; screen annually once the patient is well controlled.

items.finding: Scattered microaneurysms and dot-blot haemorrhages in the posterior pole; no cotton wool spots, venous beading, IRMA, or new vessels on the disc.
items.reason: Remember: mild NPDR = microaneurysms only; add dot-blot haemorrhages for moderate; add cotton wool spots, venous beading, or IRMA for severe NPDR; new vessels define PDR.

items.finding: Scattered red dot microaneurysms in the posterior pole; no neovascularisation, no preretinal or vitreous haemorrhage, no cotton wool spots or IRMA.
items.reason: Remember: Microaneurysms alone = mild NPDR; add haemorrhages, exudates or cotton wool spots in more than one quadrant = moderate NPDR; add IRMA, venous beading or neovascularisation = severe NPDR or PDR (4-2-1 rule).

items.finding: Absence of new vessels on the optic disc, absence of pre-retinal or vitreous haemorrhage, and no dot-blot haemorrhages or cotton wool spots in more than one quadrant.
items.reason: Remember: mild NPDR = microaneurysms only; moderate adds haemorrhages, hard exudates or cotton wool spots; severe uses the 4-2-1 rule; PDR = neovascularisation or vitreous haemorrhage.

items.finding: Dot and blot haemorrhages in all four quadrants; cotton wool spots; hard exudates near the macula; absence of new vessels or vitreous haemorrhage.
items.reason: Remember the 4-2-1 rule: haemorrhages in all 4 quadrants, venous beading in 2 or more quadrants, or IRMA in 1 quadrant defines severe NPDR, with about 50 percent risk of PDR within 1 year.

items.finding: Fibrovascular tissue arising from the optic disc; overlying haemorrhage and hazy vitreous; sudden painless visual loss in a long-standing diabetic.
items.reason: Remember: neovascularisation at the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE) = PDR; new vessels bleed easily, so sudden painless vision loss in a diabetic should prompt a search for vitreous haemorrhage and PRP.

items.finding: Elevated ridge at the vascular-avascular junction; extraretinal fibrovascular tissue; retina remains attached; preterm birth at 30 weeks with screening at 34 weeks postmenstrual age.
items.reason: Remember: Stage 1 is a flat line, Stage 2 a raised ridge, Stage 3 a ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation, and Stage 4 a partial detachment; Stage 3 with plus disease or zone I/II meets treatment thresholds.

items.finding: Elevated ridge at the vascular-avascular junction; extraretinal fibrovascular tissue; tortuous posterior pole vessels; preterm birth at 28 weeks.
items.reason: Remember: Stage 1 is a line, stage 2 is a ridge, stage 3 is a ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation, stage 4 is partial detachment, and stage 5 is total detachment.

items.finding: Elevated ridge at the vascular-avascular junction; fibrovascular tissue extending into the vitreous; preterm birth at 26 weeks with postmenstrual age 34 weeks.
items.reason: Remember: Stage 1 is a flat line, Stage 2 is a raised ridge, Stage 3 is a ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation, and Stage 4 is partial detachment; stage 3 is the key threshold for treatment in high-risk eyes.

items.finding: Raised ridge at the vascular-avascular junction; no extraretinal fibrovascular tissue; preterm birth at 30 weeks.
items.reason: Remember: Stage 1 is a flat line, stage 2 is an elevated ridge, stage 3 adds extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation, and stage 4 is partial detachment.

items.finding: Raised ridge at the vascular-avascular junction; absence of extraretinal fibrovascular tissue; preterm birth at 26 weeks with screening at 33 weeks postmenstrual age.
items.reason: Remember: stage 1 is a flat line, stage 2 is a raised ridge, stage 3 is ridge with extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation, stage 4 is partial retinal detachment, and stage 5 is total retinal detachment.

items.finding: Dense white retrolental mass; funnel-shaped retina; complete detachment; preterm birth at 31 weeks.
items.reason: Remember: ROP Stage 4 is partial detachment, Stage 5 is total funnel-shaped detachment (Stage 5 = Total, a funnel-shaped retinal fold behind the lens).

items.finding: Posterior pole involvement with the disc centrally placed; dark, ill-defined avascular posterior retina; absence of a clear ridge; tortuous irregular vessels; preterm birth at 29 weeks.
items.reason: Remember: Aggressive posterior ROP (A-ROP) affects the posterior pole with no clear ridge, progresses rapidly within days, and needs urgent treatment.

items.finding: Posterior-pole haze, tortuous dilated vessels, intraretinal haemorrhage, absent demarcation ridge, very preterm birth.
items.reason: Remember: A-ROP is posterior, rapidly progressive, lacks a clear demarcation ridge, and needs treatment within days of detection.

items.finding: Hazy posterior pole; tortuous, irregularly branching vessels; hemorrhagic lesion near vascular front; absence of clear demarcation ridge; preterm birth at 28 weeks.
items.reason: Remember: A-ROP is posterior-predominant, rapidly progressive, with plus disease and no classic staging ridge; treat urgently as it can progress to retinal detachment within days.

items.finding: Elevated grey-white detached retinal fold; visible optic disc; fibrovascular ridge arching over the posterior retina without total funnel configuration.
items.reason: Remember: Stage 4 ROP = partial retinal detachment (4A extrafoveal, 4B foveal involvement); Stage 5 = total funnel detachment.

items.finding: Funnel-shaped concave retinal elevation; posterior pull toward the macula; attached retina still visible in other sectors; preterm neonate at 27 weeks.
items.reason: Remember: ROP stage 4 = partial retinal detachment (4A extrafoveal, 4B foveal); stage 5 = total detachment.

items.finding: Elevated, funnel-shaped retina; fibrovascular ridge at the junction with vascularised retina; traction pulling the retina anteriorly with the optic disc still visible posteriorly.
items.reason: Remember: Stage 4 ROP = partial retinal detachment (4A extrafoveal, 4B foveal involvement); Stage 5 = total detachment.

items.finding: Flat pale fibrotic macular lesion; no subretinal fluid; no foveal break; normal optic disc and rim.
items.reason: Remember: a grey-white, atrophic, fibrotic macular lesion with preserved peripheral vision and a healthy disc points to a macular scar, the permanent end-stage of previous chorioretinal damage.

items.finding: Irregular depigmented fibrotic patch at the macula; chorioretinal atrophy with whitish streaks; absence of haemorrhage, exudate or subretinal fluid; residual pigmented foveal spot.
items.reason: Remember: a macular scar is an irreversible, depigmented, fibrous area of chorioretinal atrophy; it is non-progressive, so check OCT and angiography for any active choroidal neovascular membrane before labelling it as inactive.

items.finding: Round, well-demarcated dome-shaped macular elevation; absence of hemorrhage; young male with stress and steroid use; unilateral blurring with central scotoma.
items.reason: Remember: central serous chorioretinopathy is a young male, stress and steroid-associated, unilateral, self-limiting serous macular detachment; diagnose with OCT and fluorescein angiography (FA).

items.finding: Dome-shaped serous macular elevation; young male with stress and steroid use; unilateral painless blurring with metamorphopsia; normal optic disc.
items.reason: Remember: CSCR is a young male with stress or steroid use, a unilateral dome-shaped serous macular detachment on fundus, and most cases resolve within 3 months; confirm with OCT and FA/ICGA.

items.finding: Discrete creamy-white focal lesions in the posterior pole; overlying hazy retina; optic disc mildly hyperaemic; reduced vision with floaters.
items.reason: Remember: discrete yellow-white chorioretinal lesions with vitreous cells in a young patient suggest chorioretinitis, and toxoplasmosis is the commonest infectious cause.

items.finding: Large central excavation; thinned neuroretinal rim; disc margins are sharp rather than elevated; family history of glaucoma with raised IOP.
items.reason: Remember: cupping means a large cup-to-disc ratio with a thin rim; papilledema means swollen, blurred disc margins.

items.finding: Bright red, sharply demarcated, flat patch on the bulbar conjunctiva; clear cornea; normal pupil; painless with preserved vision.
items.reason: Remember: a sharply demarcated bright red patch on the bulbar conjunctiva with no pain, no discharge and normal vision is subconjunctival haemorrhage, which is usually benign and self-limiting, but check blood pressure and systemic risk factors.

items.finding: Irregular, distorted pupil; posterior synechia between iris and lens; increased lens density; ciliary flush and photophobia.
items.reason: Remember: posterior synechiae, an irregular pupil, and cells and flare in the anterior chamber with ciliary flush point to anterior uveitis; check HLA-B27 and syphilis serology.

items.finding: Diffuse milky-white opacity of the entire crystalline lens; iris and anterior chamber visible; fundus view obscured; elderly patient with progressive painless vision loss and glare.
items.reason: Remember: A dense white lens opacity in an elderly patient is an advanced (white) age-related cataract; the lens is opaque enough to block the red reflex and fundus view, and phacoemulsification is the definitive treatment.

items.dx: Intraocular lens with posterior capsule tear
items.finding: Visible IOL optic and haptic in the pupil; ragged torn posterior capsule with floating flaps; history of trauma or prior cataract surgery.
items.reason: Remember: a posterior capsule tear with an IOL in the pupil carries a high risk of vitreous prolapse, retinal detachment and IOL drop, so refer urgently.
